pages.text: "Oh... What do I do?" Bami stood still in the dining car. Dad's blue cup lay broken at their feet. Hopping on the table, Bami had knocked it with a wing.
Bami's face burned. They should tell Dad—it was his favorite morning tea cup. But their beak stayed shut. Bami quickly swept the pieces beneath the table with a wing.
Bami slipped into a window corner. Snow fell outside. Mom entered with lunchboxes, but Bami watched only the window. The car was quiet except for their thumping heart.
Mom saw Bami's unhappy face. "Your heart feels heavy?" She sat beside them and patted their back. "What might help?" Bami lowered their head.
Keeping quiet felt like a huge, poking stone on their chest. Mom saw the blue pieces and said softly, "Words make that stone disappear. Tell Dad, 'I broke it.'"
At a station, Dad came from the cab. "Tea before we go. Where's my cup?" He searched the cupboard. Bami's heart gave a thump.
Bami took a big breath and looked at Dad. "I broke your cup. And hid it under the table." They spread their wings and pointed. Say, 'I broke it.'
The heart-stone turned to soft down. Dad took a new cup from the cupboard and set it beside the pieces. "Thank you for telling me. You aren't hurt? We have another cup." He nuzzled Bami's head.
After the pieces had been swept up, Bami poured Dad tea. "One, stop when something breaks! Two, don't hide it! Three, say 'I broke it.'" Dad sipped. "This cup is lovely, too."
Mom and Dad cuddled Bami. "So brave to tell us!" Speaking instead of hiding a mistake made their heart lighter. Say, 'I broke it.' Snow fell outside, and the dining car was warm again.
